sentences.text: The storm passed in the middle of the night.

Bata woke once, in the very small hours, and heard silence — the rain had stopped, and the wind had dropped, and outside the hut there was only the small sound of the horses shifting under the overhang.
He fell asleep again quickly.
When he woke properly it was dawn, and the world outside the hut had been washed clean.
They stepped outside into cold clear morning air.
The grass had been beaten flat by the rain but was already beginning to lift.
The sky was pale and empty.
The horses were fine — wet, but calm.
Chuluun looked at Bata with mild reproach, as if to say, next time, less of that.
Odval laughed when she saw the horse's face.
It was the first time she had laughed since the storm.
Before they left, Odval led Bata up to the ovoo.
She said, "When you pass an ovoo, you walk around it three times, in the direction the sun goes, and you add a stone." She handed him a small round stone she had picked up.
She had another for herself.
"You can say anything you want as you walk.
Or you can say nothing.
It is between you and the mountain."
They walked around the ovoo three times, slowly, in the cold morning light.
Bata did not know what to say.
He thought about his great-great-grandfather, who had ridden the small saddle into a much worse storm than his.
He thought about the young horse that had come home wrapped in a man's coat.
He thought about Odval, who had known this place would be here, and had known which direction to ride when the sky went dark.
He thought, thank you.
He was not sure who he was thanking.
He put his stone on the pile anyway.
Odval put hers beside his.
They saddled the horses and untied the herd and started for home.
The nine horses moved eagerly this morning — they wanted their own pasture.
The land, freshly rained on, smelled of earth and grass and something Bata did not have a name for.
He rode at the rear again, on Chuluun, in the small old saddle, and listened to it creak beneath him.
About halfway home, Odval slowed her mare until she was riding beside him.
She said, "You did well last night.
You did not cry.
You did not panic.
You listened." Bata said, "You did the work.
I only followed." Odval said, "That is exactly right.
Following well is a skill.
The first time out, you follow.
The second time, you follow with your eyes open.
The third time, you begin to know why.
That is how it goes."
They came over the last rise a little before noon.
Bata saw the ger below — small and white against the huge green — and he saw his father walking out to meet them, one hand raised in greeting.
Batbayar had been worried.
Bata could see it in the way he walked.
But when he saw the horses were all there, and Odval was riding easily, and Bata was upright in the small saddle, he stopped worrying.
He waved instead.
He was smiling.
They drove the horses into the corral.
Batbayar took Chuluun's reins as Bata dismounted.
He looked at his son, then at the small saddle, then at his mother.
He did not say anything for a moment.
Then he said, quietly, in Odval's direction, "So he has it now." Odval said, "He has it now."
That evening, after supper, Odval told Bata to hang the small saddle back on its peg on the north wall of the ger.
He climbed onto a stool and lifted it up.
It fit into the same worn hollow in the wood that it had rested in for a hundred and twenty years.
He climbed back down.
Odval was watching him.
She said, "It stays there now until you ride again.
When you do, you take it down.
When you come back, you put it up.
That is how it has always worked.
Your father did this.
His father did this.
His father did this.
His father did this.
Now you."
Bata looked at the saddle.
It was small and dark and old, and the small triangle brand on the underside faced the wall now, and could not be seen.
He did not need to see it.
He knew it was there.
Outside the ger, the summer evening was long and pale.
Somewhere in the middle distance, a horse whinnied — one of the racing yearlings, restless, wanting to run.
In three weeks it would run at Naadam.
Bata would be there, riding beside his father.
But that was in three weeks.
Tonight, he was home.
The saddle was on its peg.
The wind had dropped.
And his grandmother, in the warm circle of firelight, was pouring another bowl of tea.
